```rust
}

// Levenberg-Marquardt for min sum r(p)^2, hand-written (R: nls / nls.lm, Python: least_squares)
fn levmar(r: &dyn Fn(&[f64]) -> Vec<f64>, p0: &[f64]) -> Vec<f64> {
    let ss = |p: &[f64]| -> f64 { let v = r(p); if v.iter().all(|x| x.is_finite()) { v.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum() } else { f64::INFINITY } };
    let (mut p, mut mu) = (p0.to_vec(), 1e-3);
    for _ in 0..500 {
        let j = jacobian(r, &p);                     // Jacobian of the residuals
        let rv = DVector::from_vec(r(&p));
        let jtj = j.transpose() * &j;
        let g = j.transpose() * &rv;
        loop {
            let a = &jtj + DMatrix::from_diagonal(&jtj.diagonal()) * mu;
            let step = a.lu().solve(&(-&g)).unwrap();
            let pn: Vec<f64> = p.iter().zip(step.iter()).map(|(a, b)| a + b).collect();
            if ss(&pn) <= ss(&p) {
                let small = step.norm() < 1e-12 * (1.0 + DVector::from_vec(p.clone()).norm());
                p = pn;
                mu = (mu / 10.0).max(1e-12);
                if small { return p; }
                break;
            }
            mu *= 10.0;
            if mu > 1e12 { return p; }
        }
    }
    p
}

// Residuals y - C(t) for the one-compartment model at the sample times ts
fn resid(ts: &[f64], ys: &[f64]) -> impl Fn(&[f64]) -> Vec<f64> {
    let (ts, ys) = (ts.to_vec(), ys.to_vec());
    move |p: &[f64]| ts.iter().zip(&ys).map(|(ti, yi)| yi - bateman(*ti, p[0], p[1], p[2])).collect()
}
fn sse(r: &dyn Fn(&[f64]) -> Vec<f64>, p: &[f64]) -> f64 { r(p).iter().map(|x| x * x).sum() }

// predicted SE of log ka, log ke, log V for sample times ts, at a guessed theta
fn se_design(ts: &[f64], p: [f64; 3], sigma: f64) -> Vec<f64> {
    let f = |lp: &[f64]| -> Vec<f64> { ts.iter().map(|t| bateman(*t, lp[0].exp(), lp[1].exp(), lp[2].exp())).collect() };
    let lp: Vec<f64> = p.iter().map(|x| x.ln()).collect();
    let j = jacobian(&f, &lp);
    let c = (j.transpose() * &j).try_inverse().unwrap();
    (0..3).map(|i| sigma * c[(i, i)].sqrt()).collect()
}

fn main() {
    let designs: [(&str, [f64; 6]); 3] = [("late", [3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0]),
        ("early", [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 12.0]), ("peak", [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 12.0])];
    for (name, ts) in designs.iter() {
        let se = se_design(ts, [1.0, 0.2, 20.0], 0.1);
        println!("{:6} {:.3} {:.3} {:.3}", name, se[0], se[1], se[2]);
    }
    // (b) prior on log ka (centre log 1.2, SD tau), sparse data, noise SD 0.1
    for tau in [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0] {
        let res = |lp: &[f64]| -> Vec<f64> {
            let mut r: Vec<f64> = TT[6..].iter().zip(&Y[6..])
                .map(|(t, y)| (y - bateman(*t, lp[0].exp(), lp[1].exp(), lp[2].exp())) / 0.1).collect();
            r.push((lp[0] - 1.2_f64.ln()) / tau);
            r
        };
        let lp = levmar(&res, &[0.0, 0.2_f64.ln(), 20.0_f64.ln()]);
        let ja = jacobian(&res, &lp);
        let c = (ja.transpose() * &ja).try_inverse().unwrap();
        println!("tau {:.2}  ka {:.3}  se_logka {:.3}", tau, lp[0].exp(), c[(0, 0)].sqrt());
    }
}

// Output:
// late   0.398 0.115 0.061
// early  0.101 0.087 0.059
// peak   0.116 0.101 0.059
// tau 0.10  ka 1.197  se_logka 0.098
// tau 0.25  ka 1.182  se_logka 0.225
// tau 0.50  ka 1.156  se_logka 0.350
// tau 1.00  ka 1.134  se_logka 0.428
// tau 2.00  ka 1.125  se_logka 0.455
```

:::

Before any experiment, the late design predicts an SE of 0.40 for $\log k_a$ (a factor 1.5 either way, and the profile in C5 shows it is really unbounded), while the early design gives 0.10 with the same six samples, and even improves $k_e$. The peak design is nearly as good: samples at 1 and 2 h already carry most of the absorption information. With a prior, the SE of $\log k_a$ is always a little below $\tau$ when $\tau \le 0.5$: the estimate is mostly prior, and $\hat k_a$ stays near the prior centre 1.2. For large $\tau$ the SE approaches 0.46, the linearised SE of the data alone (with $\sigma = 0.1$), which the profile showed to be meaningless on the upper side. A prior is only informative about the data when the posterior SE is clearly smaller than $\tau$.

:::

## Where this leads

- **Part 10, [*Constraints and linear programming*](../constrained-lp/lec.qmd):** bounds such as $k_a > k_e$ or $F \le 1$ as constraints in the optimiser, and what the Lagrange multipliers of active bounds say.
- **The capstone** (if used): fit an ODE model to a real time course and report what is determined, using the checklist of the lecture (multistart, SVD of $J$, profiles, prediction uncertainty).
- We linearised (Wald SEs) and profiled with a $\chi^2_1$ threshold, both large-sample approximations. Bootstrap and Bayesian sampling (MCMC) give uncertainty without them; they need many model fits, which is where fast and robust fitting ([*Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting*](../nonlinear-least-squares/lec.qmd)) pays off.
- Structural identifiability can also be decided symbolically, before any data, for ODE models of moderate size (differential algebra, as in the tools DAISY or StructuralIdentifiability.jl). We did it by hand and from the rank of $J$.
